title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline against a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on intent-driven network configuration tasks. The study used gpt-5-mini under two conditions (baseline one‑shot; guarded verifier‑assisted), a deterministic NetOps validator and Mininet-style emulation, and a preregistered binary episode success rule (verifier accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks (two topology clusters: edge/core) we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.99750); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.00000). The paired-success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502 (95% bootstrap CI [0.0000, 0.005838]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Under this controlled emulation and task set we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline. We report deterministic execution artifacts, discuss failure‑mode observations, and note key limitations (near‑ceiling task solvability, single LLM, emulator fidelity). The full preregistration (rX4f7-1), execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and disclosure are archived with this submission.

sections.introduction: Operational automation increasingly uses generative LLMs to translate natural‑language operator intent into device configurations. Prior surveys and systems work argue that operational reliability depends less on the base model and more on the surrounding orchestration, verifiers, and assurance machinery [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair architectures have been proposed to reduce LLM-produced semantic and safety errors for executable artifacts (e.g., NL→temporal logic, topologies, Kubernetes manifests) by iterating generation against deterministic checkers [3–5]. Despite these proposals, there is little publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence quantifying whether a verifier‑assisted pipeline measurably improves binary operational success rates compared with a one‑shot generation baseline under controlled emulation. We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted LLM workflows on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered experimental design and archived execution artifacts (study rX4f7-1); (2) a paired analysis of one‑shot versus verifier‑assisted pipelines using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator; (3) a transparent failure‑mode and limitations analysis grounded in the run artifacts.
sections.related_work: Work on agentic NetOps and AIOps emphasizes that trustworthy automation requires tool scaffolding, evidence traces, and assurance contracts rather than relying on the LLM alone [1,6]. Several recent system proposals demonstrate verifier‑guided NL→formal/artifact pipelines: verifier‑grounded NL→CTL work that uses model checking in the loop [3]; intent→topology compilers that apply schema constraints and post‑generation checking [4]; and domain tools that combine deterministic validators with LLMs for configuration or misconfiguration detection [5,7]. Empirical studies of LLM failure modes (hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, prompt‑injection) motivate guarded architectures and runtime auditing [8–10]. Surveys call for workflow‑centered evaluation of multi‑step agentic systems (trace quality, rollback/canary behavior, and end‑to‑end safety metrics) rather than one‑shot QA benchmarks [1,6]. Our study situates within this literature by providing a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation that measures a binary operational success metric in a controlled emulation.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and scope: The study was preregistered (rX4f7-1) before execution. The benchmark (NetOpsTraceBench_v1) comprises 1,200 paired intent→config tasks (600 'edge', 600 'core'), public synthetic tasks with deterministic provenance tags, and vendor-agnostic canonical commands rendered for the emulator. Inclusion/exclusion, contamination detection thresholds, stopping rules, seeds, analysis code, and failure treatments were frozen in the preregistration. Pipelines tested: (A) Baseline one‑shot: single LLM call to produce device configuration; (B) Guarded verifier‑assisted: same initial candidate plus at most one automated repair iteration driven by the deterministic validator. LLM and infra: model requested = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed parsing, intent‑constraint checks, and emulator preflight. Success definition (preregistered): an episode is a binary success iff (1) the validator accepts the final configuration, (2) emulator execution produced no availability degradation exceeding the preregistered threshold, and (3) no automatic rollback event occurred. Execution: planned model calls = 2,400 (one shared initial generation per pair plus up to one repair in guarded), maximum_model_calls enforced. Analysis plan: primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = paired two‑sided Wilcoxon signed‑rank (nonparametric) with paired bootstrap 95% CI (frozen seeds); secondary descriptors and exploratory failure‑mode counts reported descriptively. All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code were archived.
sections.results: Execution summary: planned pairs = 1,200; completed pairs = 1,199 (completed episodes = 2,398; failed episodes = 2). Model calls used = 1,203; repair-stage calls observed = 3; artifact manifest available (artifact_count = 8,408). Primary confirmatory result (pre-specified): complete_pair_count = 1,199; baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline success rate = 0.9974979149); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded success rate = 1.0). Paired counts (contingency): n11 = 1,196; n10 = 3 (guarded success, baseline failure); n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Estimated paired-success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Bootstrap 95% percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) = [0.0000, 0.0058381985]. Secondary and exploratory observations: (i) the guarded pipeline invoked automated repair only three times in this run; (ii) the task generator produced predominantly medium–hard deterministic tasks for which the LLM produced the required sequences in the initial generation for the vast majority of cases; (iii) deterministic validator traces and emulator state snapshots are provided for representative tasks (see execution artifacts). No post‑preregistration deviations were recorded.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The preregistered primary test did not find a statistically significant improvement in binary episode success for the verifier‑assisted pipeline under the chosen tasks and emulation: the observed effect size was small (≈0.25 percentage points) and compatible with sampling fluctuation (p = 0.25). Two operationally important interpretations follow. First, near‑ceiling initial generation success (≈99.75%) limits the headroom for a verifier to improve the binary success metric in this task corpus; when the baseline is already near perfect under the chosen deterministic validator and emulator, measurable gains are necessarily small. Second, the guarded pipeline was exercised for repair only three times—suggesting either the validator accepted a large fraction of initial candidates or the task set did not stress semantic failure modes the verifier is intended to catch. Implications: controlled, preregistered paired evaluations are necessary to avoid optimistic claims about verifier benefit, but benchmark construction must purposefully include adversarial, ambiguous, and distribution‑shifted cases to stress the guarded machinery. Relation to prior work: our negative result in this narrowly defined setting complements system proposals advocating verifier scaffolding [3–5] and emphasizes that gains depend on task difficulty, verifier strictness, and emulator fidelity [1,6].
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired NetOpsTraceBench run comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted LLM pipelines for NL→configuration on 1,199 completed pairs. Under these controlled emulation conditions with gpt-5-mini and the supplied deterministic validator, we observed no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline. The run artifacts are archived and fully reproducible under the provided manifests. Future work should broaden model families, increase adversarial and ambiguous tasks, vary verifier strictness, and compare emulator outcomes against higher‑fidelity production traces to evaluate operational impact more robustly.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet-style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, transient telemetry, vendor idiosyncrasies).
Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change results.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct operational generalization.
Sample and effect-size sensitivity: the observed small absolute effect (≈0.25 percentage points) is within the preregistered sensitivity bounds and does not support broad production claims.
